contributions.statement: For read-only developer questions over a repository you can index, start from a flat agent with an embedding index plus file-read and repo-structure tools rather than a planner that delegates grep exploration to a same-model sub-agent: on 720 paired questions the flat index agent passed 65.2% vs 46.2% (5.6 to 49.6 points ahead on each of four models) at 1.5x to 24x lower cost per correct answer.
contributions.evidence: Tables 3-4 and Sec. 5.1-5.2: McNemar and Wilcoxon with FDR correction, pass-threshold sweep 50-90, repository-level bootstrap, 14 of 15 repos. Index build cost under $1 for all 15 repos. Caveats: one run at temperature 0; the arms bundle retrieval tool, delegation and todo planning; both are LangChain defaults with 900 s / 80-step caps counted as failures; Python only; the 49.6-point Gemini 3 Flash gap dominates the pooled number.

contributions.statement: Do not accept a delegated exploration sub-agent's condensed prose result as grounded unless it carries file:line evidence that the planner or developer can check: 41.8% of the delegating agent's failures (414 of 990, about 14% of its runs) were planner-to-sub-agent hand-off breakdowns, and about 91% of those still returned a fluent, confident answer.
contributions.evidence: Sec. 6, Table 5 (no-answer share 9.4% for coordination breakdowns). Mechanisms were coded by Claude Sonnet 4.6 and checked on 400 stratified failures (two authors kappa 0.78 on mechanism; 0.82 consensus vs automatic). Caveats: the coder sees the judge's rationale; the category exists only for the delegating arm and may absorb sub-agent search misses; the file:line remedy is not tested here.

contributions.statement: Treat codebase QA agent answers as drafts that need developer-checkable citations whichever design is used: even the better arm fully passed only 48-89% of questions per model, and in both designs 42-48% of failures were confident answers about the wrong file or mechanism and 8.5-14.9% wrongly claimed the code does not exist.
contributions.evidence: Table 3 (Semantic pass 48.4, 54.2, 89.3, 68.8%) and Table 5 symptom block (wrong entity or mechanism 48.2% / 42.3%; premise denial 14.9% / 8.5%). Python SWE-QA on frozen snapshots, a best case for an index.

contributions.statement: When an LLM judge grades competing agent designs on codebase questions with reference answers, validate it against blind human graders on about 100 stratified answers per condition and report agreement per arm: three engineers on 800 answers gave kappa 0.74 overall (Pearson 0.83, mean absolute difference 5.2/100) but 0.69 on the delegating arm's longer answers vs 0.78 on the retrieval arm's.
contributions.evidence: Sec. 4 and Table 2 (panel Fleiss kappa 0.81 [0.78, 0.84]; per-arm CIs [0.63, 0.75] vs [0.72, 0.84] barely overlap). The judge (Claude Sonnet 4.6) is from a different vendor than the answering models. Validation was run once, not repeated over time.

contributions.statement: Do not assume grep-style delegated exploration overtakes an embedding index on large repositories: the index agent's lead narrowed with repository size (Spearman -0.69 across 15 repos) but was still 13.7 points on the largest, about 861k lines.
contributions.evidence: Sec. 5.1, Fig. 10, pooled scores across four models; one repository per size point, Python only, single run; django (mid-sized) was the only repo where the delegating arm led (+3.0).

reason: This is a careful paired comparison with a human-validated judge and human-validated failure coding. Four contributions survive at moderate strength. A flat index-plus-read agent is a better default than LangChain-style delegated grep exploration for read-only QA. Delegated prose hand-offs fail silently. QA answers need checkable citations in both designs. Judge agreement should be validated per arm. All are bundle-level results on Python and LangChain defaults, so they transfer to the team's Java repos and hosts only indirectly, apart from the judge-validation practice.
